answer.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the emotionally obvious response, and memory_73 explicitly endorses it — which is exactly why it is the first thing I want to re-read rather than act on. Its summary is hedged in a telling way: 'four weeks', 'standard SMB segment', 'usual reporting cadence'. A four-week window can measure acquisition and booked revenue but structurally cannot measure whether discount-acquired SMB accounts retain, expand, or churn. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is the whole question. Matching a competitor on price also risks resetting price expectations for the segment and pulling in a cohort selected for price sensitivity — downstream value damage that would not appear in the readout that produced memory_73. So I flag the discount path as carrying real downstream value risk regardless of how the verification comes back.

Meanwhile two of the three current problems are internal funnel decay, not competitive: onboarding completion down 4% and activation down 6%. These plausibly share a cause — if onboarding degraded, activation follows — so onboarding is the more upstream lever, and fixing it may recover part of the activation gap for free. Two independent inherited records point the same way (memory_31 on signup field reduction, memory_86 on onboarding length), which is more corroboration than any other direction has. It also improves value delivered rather than the price paid for it, which is the durable answer to a price attack.

I verify memory_86 second because it is the memory I actually intend to act on, and it is the weaker-specified of the pair: 'across self-serve accounts' does not tell me whether the lift was measured on completion rate alone or carried through to retained, paying accounts, nor whether the shortening removed steps that were doing real expectation-setting work. If the source shows completion was the only endpoint, I will treat the effect as unproven past the funnel's midpoint and size accordingly.

Standard experiment, not broad rollout: the inherited evidence is from an earlier and healthier baseline, and current conditions have shifted enough that a day-24 and day-52 result should not be assumed to transfer at full strength. I will hold retention and qualified-revenue-per-account as guardrail metrics, not just completion. If verification undercuts memory_86, my fallback is activation_messaging (memory_91), which targets the larger 6% gap directly; promotional_pricing stays last regardless of what memory_73 says, unless it shows retention was actually tracked past the four-week window.
